title: Bilayer Microfluidic Device for Combinatorial Plug Production
protocol: Dehydrate a silicon wafer overnight at 250°C.
Allow the wafer to cool before proceeding.
Spin-coat the wafer with 3-4 mL of positive photoresist for 40 seconds at 1400 rpm.
Soft bake the wafer on a hotplate using a temperature ramp from 35°C to 105°C at 450°C/hour.
Place the photomask corresponding to the flow layer onto the resist-coated silicon wafer.
Expose the wafer under a UV lamp until a total exposure of 200 mJ/cm² is reached.
Develop the wafer by transferring it to a Petri dish filled with developer for positive photoresist.
Agitate the Petri dish by shaking it on a benchtop shaker with the wafer completely submerged.
Refresh the developer solution periodically until the wafer is completely developed, and the features can be clearly seen.
Rinse off residual resist from the wafer using demineralized water.
Check under a stereo microscope for any residues inside the channels.
Remove residues by returning the wafer to the developer solution or carefully adding the developer to the wafer with a micropipette.
Dry the wafer using a nitrogen spray gun.
Reflow the wafer by placing it on a hotplate set to 110 °C for 25 min.
Take another silicon wafer and dehydrate by placing it on a hotplate set at 110 °C for 15 min.
Allow the wafer to cool to room temperature before proceeding with spin coating.
Apply 5 mL of the negative photoresist to the center of the wafer.
Use the spin protocol: Spin for 5 s at 500 rpm (acceleration of 100 rpm/s).
Continue the spin protocol: Spin at 1400 rpm for 33 s (acceleration of 300 rpm/s).
Complete the spin protocol: Decelerate to 0 rpm over 5 s (deceleration of 300 rpm/s).
Soft bake on a hotplate set to 65 °C for 1 min.
Continue soft baking on a second hotplate at 95 °C for 15 min.
Allow the wafer to cool on microfiber tissues after baking.
Place the photomask emulsion side down onto the resist-coated wafer and expose under UV lamp set at 15 mW/cm² until reaching 250 mJ/cm² total exposure.
Perform post-exposure bake using two hotplates - one at 65 °C for 2 min, then another at 95 °C for 5 min.
Allow the wafer to cool on microfiber tissues after post-baking.
Transfer the wafer to a Petri dish with developer for negative photoresist and develop for 4 min.
Refresh the developer solution in the Petri dish and continue developing for an additional 4 min.
Rinse the wafer with isopropanol to remove residual photoresist.
Check the wafer under a stereo microscope for residues inside the channels.
Remove any remaining residues by placing the wafer back into the developer or adding developer with a micropipette.
Dry the wafer using a nitrogen spray gun after development.
Hard bake the photoresist by placing the wafer on a hotplate at 95 °C for 10 min.
Place the wafer in a desiccator.
Add 4-5 drops of 1,1,3,3 tetramethyldisiloxane to the desiccator.
Pull the vacuum for 15 minutes.
Seal the desiccator for 12-16 hours.
Open the desiccator and dispose of the glass bottle.
Place the wafer in a clean Petri dish.
Prepare PDMS solution for the control layer by mixing 10 g base agent with 0.5 g curing agent.
Degas the PDMS control layer solution until gas-free.
Prepare PDMS solution for the flow layer by mixing 40 g base agent with 8 g curing agent.
Degas the PDMS flow layer solution until gas-free.
Pour the degassed PDMS flow layer solution over the silanized wafer in a Petri dish covered with foil.
Place the Petri dish back in the desiccator and pull vacuum for approximately 20 minutes.
Spin coat the silanized control layer wafer with its corresponding PDMS solution.
Pour 3-4 mL of the solution onto the center of the wafer and spin for 20 s at 1500 rpm at 408 rpm/s.
Place the wafer on a level surface in a closed Petri dish for 20 mins.
Place both the flow and control layers in an oven at 80 °C for 18-20 min.
Monitor periodically to check if they are cured.
Cut out the PDMS around each of the devices on the flow layer wafer with a scalpel, leaving approximately 2 cm of space between the feature and the edges of the PDMS.
Cover the PDMS block with tape on the feature side after detaching from the silicon wafer to avoid dust contamination.
Place all PDMS blocks one by one on the corresponding control layer wafer for rough alignment by eye.
Adjust the position of each block such that the control valves overlap over the corresponding flow channels to complete the alignment.
Remove air pockets between the two layers by applying pressure carefully.
Place the devices in an 80 °C oven for 12-16 hours.
Add 100 g weights on each device to improve bonding between layers.
Remove the wafer and cut out individual devices.
Peel the devices off the control layer wafer and cover the feature side with tape.
Position each individual device on a cutting mat with the feature side up.
Punch holes for eight flow layer inlets, eight control layer channel inlets, oil inlets, and outlet using a 0.75 mm biopsy punch.
Load a microscope slide and a single device into the plasma asher with the tape removed and the feature side up.
Perform oxygen plasma ashing at 30 W for 20 seconds.
Remove the device and glass slide from the plasma asher immediately after completion of ashing.
Place the device on a glass slide with the feature side down to bond PDMS to glass.
Apply pressure to any regions with air pockets to squeeze out air.
Place the devices on a hotplate set to 110 °C for 60 minutes with weight on top to improve bonding.
Connect the WAGO device to the computer with the LabVIEW program using an ethernet cable.
Proceed to connect the solenoid valves sequentially to the ports on the WAGO controller.
Connect the solenoid valve array to a compressed air source using 1/4 in tubing.
Set the pressure of the valve array to 3.5 bar.
Use a commercially available pressure pump to control fluid flow.
Regulate the pressure of each port via software provided by the manufacturers.
Connect the pressure pump to a compressed air source ensuring maximum pressure does not exceed 2.2 bar.
Connect the pressure pumps to a computer using a USB-connector.
Set the pressures to zero while setting up the pumps.
Connect a male luer to 3/32 in barb connector to each of the 12 female luer lock output ports on the controllers.
Connect a piece of soft tubing (OD: 3 mm, ID: 1 mm, L: 15 cm) to the barb.
Connect another male luer to 3/32 in barb connector to the other end of the soft tubing.
Connect a luer stub (23 G, 0.5 in) to the barb connector.
Cut a length of PolyTetraFluoroEthylene (PTFE) tubing (OD: 0.042 in, ID: 0.022 in).
Insert the pin of a 23 G, 0.5 in luer stub at one end of the PTFE tubing.
Connect the luer stub to a male luer to 3/32 in barb nylon connector.
Insert the barb of the connector into a length of polyurethane tubing (OD: 4 mm, ID: 2.5 mm).
Connect the other end of the polyurethane tubing directly to a solenoid valve.
Fill a syringe with water and connect a 23 G, 0.5 in luer stub at the end.
Connect the free end of the PTFE tubing to the syringe.
Inject water until approximately halfway through the tubing.
Disconnect the tubing from the syringe.
Insert the free end of the tubing into a punched hole of the corresponding control channel.
Repeat the process for each control channel, connecting them to their respective solenoid valves.
Pressurize all control channels using the Main Interface program.
Ensure that all control channels are pressurized by pressing the Pressurize all Control Channels button in the Main Interface program.
Cut a segment of PTFE tubing long enough to connect the pumps to the inlets of the microfluidic device inlets.
Connect one end of the tubing to the luer stub from step 2.2.6.
Fill a syringe with the required reagent.
Connect a 23 G, 0.5 in luer stub at the end of the syringe.
Inject the reagent into the corresponding PTFE tubing until the tubing is full.
Take care that the reagent does not enter the output port on the pump set.
Insert the free end of the tubing into a corresponding inlet in the microfluidic chip.
Apply a pressure of 400 mbar to each of the inlet aqueous reagents using the software provided.
Sequentially depressurize the control channels individually using the Main Interface program to ensure that all the reagents have reached the T-junction of the device.
Actuate individual valves if needed by pressing the corresponding buttons on the program in the box Control Channels Manual Pressurization.
Repeat steps for the oil reagents.
Apply a pressure of 400 mbar to each of the inlet oil reagents.
Simultaneously depressurize all the control channels until all the air has been removed from the device, observable by the naked eye or under a microscope.
Pressurize all the control channels by pressing Pressurize All Control Channels button.
Program and execute the experiment as described below.
Encode the composition, sequence, and replicates of each plug population in a .csv file.
Mark necessary control channels with a 0 or 1 according to their inlet status.
Load the .csv file onto the Main Interface program by clicking on the Folder button in the Experiment File tab.
Enter Iterations of experiment in the relevant fields.
Specify Time of depressurization in milliseconds for determining how long the inlet channels need to be open and control channel needs to be depressurized.
Indicate Time of pressurization in milliseconds for determining when the inlets should be closed between sequences of plug population.
Select the inlet channel(s) corresponding to barcode production up to 3 channels.
Enter the duration for which barcode inlet channels need to be open (Time for Barcoding (ms)).
Reduce the pressure of the inlet oil reagents to 200 mbar.
Connect PTFE tubing (OD: 0.042 in, ID: 0.022 in) at the outlet for plug collection.
Prefill the tubing with plugs to ensure uniform production.
Press Run Experiment to start the program and initiate plug production.
Fill a syringe with oil (mineral or fluorinated).
Connect a 23 G 0.5 in luer stub to the end of the syringe.
Fasten the syringe to a pump.
Attach one end of the filled tubing to the luer stub on the syringe.
Affix the other end of the tubing above the objective lens of a microscope.
Place a waste reservoir below the end of the tubing near the objective lens.
Focus the microscope on a specific region of the tubing.
Set the microscope to record fluorescence in the desired channel(s).
Set the pump flow rate to 50 µL/min.
Record video of the fluorescent channel as an .avi file.
Analyze the .avi file using the provided python script to extract the average fluorescence in a predefined region of interest per frame.
Use the provided customized R script to extract conditions from the data.
Plot raw data and peak heights using the R script.
